title: Multiplicative Jordan decomposition and its linear and tensor compatibility
statement: Let $K$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field], meaning every nonconstant polynomial in $K[T]$ has a root in $K$. For every finite-dimensional $K$-vector space $V$ and invertible $K$-linear map $A:V\to V$, there are unique invertible $K$-linear maps $A_s,A_u:V\to V$ such that $A=A_sA_u=A_uA_s$, $A_s$ is diagonalizable (there is a basis of eigenvectors over $K$), and $(A_u-\mathrm{id}_V)^N=0$ for some integer $N\geq1$. These maps are called its semisimple and unipotent parts. If $W$ is another finite-dimensional $K$-vector space, $B:W\to W$ is invertible, and $f:V\to W$ is $K$-linear with $fA=Bf$, then $fA_s=B_sf$ and $fA_u=B_uf$. For the automorphism $A\otimes B$ on $V\otimes_K W$, one has $(A\otimes B)_s=A_s\otimes B_s$ and $(A\otimes B)_u=A_u\otimes B_u$. Here the tensor product is the vector space universal for $K$-bilinear maps out of $V\times W$, and $(A\otimes B)(v\otimes w)=Av\otimes Bw$. Composition is the product of linear maps. The zero vector space is allowed.

source.place: Theorem 9.11, printed pp.168--169; Propositions 9.13 and 9.15, printed p.169; algebraically closed specialization (semisimple means diagonalizable).

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-generalized-eigenspace-direct-sum] to $A$. Write $V_a=E_a(A)$ and $d=\max(1,\dim_K V)$. Thus $V=\bigoplus_a V_a$ and $(A-a)^d$ vanishes on $V_a$. Each $V_a$ is $A$-stable, since $A$ commutes with $(A-a)^d$. If $v\in V_0$, then $A^d v=0$ and invertibility gives $v=0$. Consequently all nonzero primary spaces have $a\ne0$. When $V=0$, take both factors to be its identity; their uniqueness, the intertwiner assertions involving zero, and the tensor assertions involving zero follow from the fact that every linear map from or to the zero space is zero. In the remaining steps we can therefore take the spaces under consideration to be nonzero.

source.place: Proposition 9.9, p.167; Theorem 9.11, p.168, first paragraph (algebraically closed case).

proof.text: Define $S$ and $S^{-1}$ on $V_a$ by multiplication by $a$ and $a^{-1}$, respectively. Unique finite primary expansions [lem-sfb-generalized-eigenspace-direct-sum] make these linear maps well defined and mutually inverse. Choose a basis in each nonzero $V_a$; their union is a basis of $V$ by the direct-sum property, and consists of $S$-eigenvectors. On $V_a$, the maps $A$ and $S$ commute. Set $U=S^{-1}A=AS^{-1}$; it is invertible, $SU=US=A$, and on $V_a$ one has $U-1=a^{-1}(A-a)$. Hence $(U-1)^d=0$ on every primary space and therefore on $V$. This constructs the required factors, with $A_s=S$ and $A_u=U$.

source.place: Theorem 9.11, p.168, construction on the primary spaces; nilpotence written explicitly.

proof.text: For uniqueness suppose $A=S'U'=U'S'$ is another such pair, with $(U'-1)^r=0$, $r\geq1$. Take any vector $v$ of an eigenbasis for $S'$, with $S'v=av$. Since $S'$ commutes with $U'$, the whole $S'$-eigenspace of eigenvalue $a$ is $U'$-stable. On it $A-a=a(U'-1)$, so $(A-a)^r v=a^r(U'-1)^r v=0$. Thus $v\in E_a(A)$ as defined in [lem-sfb-generalized-eigenspace-direct-sum], and the constructed $S$ acts on $v$ as $a$. Therefore $Sv=S'v$ on an entire basis, whence $S=S'$ and $U=S^{-1}A=U'$. This is the uniqueness argument of 9.11 in primary-space coordinates; it avoids assuming without proof that two decompositions are simultaneously diagonalizable.

source.place: Theorem 9.11, p.168, uniqueness, specialized to the primary-space construction.

proof.text: Suppose $fA=Bf$. Induction on $n$ gives $(B-a)^n f=f(A-a)^n$ for every $a\in K$ and $n\geq0$: the initial identity is $(B-a)f=f(A-a)$ and the successor step multiplies it once more. Consequently $f(E_a(A))\subseteq E_a(B)$ by the defining formula in [lem-sfb-generalized-eigenspace-direct-sum]. On this image both $fA_s$ and $B_sf$ equal $af$, so they agree on all of $V$. Multiplying $fA_s=B_sf$ on the left by $B_s^{-1}$ and on the right by $A_s^{-1}$ gives $fA_s^{-1}=B_s^{-1}f$. It follows that $fA_u=fA_s^{-1}A=B_s^{-1}Bf=B_uf$.

source.place: Proposition 9.13, p.169; power intertwining and the inverse calculation expanded.

proof.text: Put $C=A\otimes B$. The tensor space is finite dimensional: if $(v_i)$ and $(w_j)$ are finite bases, then the finitely many $v_i\otimes w_j$ span, by bilinearity and the universal property. Also $C$ is invertible with inverse $A^{-1}\otimes B^{-1}$, as checked on pure tensors. For $v\in E_a(A)$ and $w\in E_b(B)$ put $d=\max(1,\dim V)$, $e=\max(1,\dim W)$, and let $H_{a,b}$ be the span of these pure tensors. On this subspace set $X=(A-a)\otimes B$ and $Y=a\,\mathrm{id}_V\otimes(B-b)$. Both preserve $H_{a,b}$; they commute, $C-ab=X+Y$, and $X^d=Y^e=0$ there by the dimension bounds of [lem-sfb-generalized-eigenspace-direct-sum]. Expanding $(X+Y)^{d+e}$ by distributivity, each word can be reordered to $X^iY^{d+e-i}$ and vanishes, since either $i\geq d$ or $d+e-i\geq e$. Thus $H_{a,b}\subseteq E_{ab}(C)$. This calculation uses no division by integers and works in every characteristic.

source.place: Proposition 9.15, p.169, inclusion of the tensor of primary spaces in the primary space of product eigenvalue, expanded.

proof.text: On $H_{a,b}$ the constructed $C_s$ acts as multiplication by $ab$, because $H_{a,b}\subseteq E_{ab}(C)$. The map $A_s\otimes B_s$ also acts as multiplication by $ab$ there. These subspaces span $V\otimes W$: expand each factor of a pure tensor into its finite primary sum by [lem-sfb-generalized-eigenspace-direct-sum] applied to $A$ and to $B$ and use bilinearity; pure tensors span by the universal property. Hence $C_s=A_s\otimes B_s$. Its inverse is $A_s^{-1}\otimes B_s^{-1}$ by evaluation on pure tensors, and therefore $C_u=C_s^{-1}C=(A_s^{-1}A)\otimes(B_s^{-1}B)=A_u\otimes B_u$. Equality on pure tensors proves the middle tensor identity. This proves both tensor assertions for the unique parts from the preceding steps.

source.place: Proposition 9.15, p.169, equality of semisimple parts and recovery of unipotent parts.

proof_origin.place: Proposition 9.9 and Theorem 9.11 (algebraically closed case), printed pp.167-168; Propositions 9.13 and 9.15, printed p.169. The routine uniqueness and tensor-primary calculations are expanded in coordinates.
